podcasts.name: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Delayed Commercial Success and Licensing
podcast.body: "What I Like About You" was an initial commercial disappointment, not breaking the Top 40 upon its January 1980 release. Its massive success came a year later, driven by heavy rotation of its video on MTV. This led to the song being extensively licensed for various uses, from the Los Angeles Dodgers to Barbie dolls, SeaWorld, and numerous movies and TV shows, generating substantial revenue for the band. "It wasn't until a video started getting played on this new thing called MTV a year later that it began to have any real impact."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Image and Genre Perception
podcast.body: The Romantics, a Detroit-based band, were known for dressing in red leather. Initially, they perceived themselves as more aligned with punk rock or new wave. However, their music ultimately leaned heavily into the Powerpop sound, demonstrating the genre's pervasive influence at the turn of the decade. "This month after Nick Lowe and the NAC were having hits with their brand of Powerpop came these four guys from Detroit, all dressed in red leather."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Contemporary Powerpop Sound
xref.body: Recorded in 1972, their song "Roadrunner" is noted for sounding "every bit as modern powerpop as anything by the strokes or slone, the new pranographers, the Danny Warhol's, Jimmy Eat World, and even the Go-Ghosts, and the knack and blondie and the Romantics," demonstrating its ahead-of-its-time quality. "It was recorded in 1972, and it is every bit as modern powerpop as anything by the strokes or slone, the new pranographers, the Danny Warhol's, Jimmy Eat World, and even the Go-Ghosts, and the knack and blondie and the Romantics."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
